1.note: Aristotle, Meteorologica II (on earthquakes, where Anaxagoras' view is discussed).

2.note: Identified as Leucippus, whom pseudo-Plutarch credits with the drum-shaped earth.

4.he: בראשון מספרי דרושיו סימן ע' עקר א'
4.note: Apparently Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 70, a. 1, ad 3; identification of the work is inferred from the description.

5.note: The chapter number follows a medieval Latin/Hebrew division of De caelo; kept as given.

6.note: Alfonso de Ulloa, author of a Vita of Charles V (Venice 1560).

7.note: The place-name is the author's conjecture from Ptolemy's tables; the identification of this 'Kartara' is uncertain.

8.note: The title of the Pesikta section is obscure; rendered literally.

9.note: The sense of the argument (whether Maimonides would or would not mention the lower hemisphere's inhabitants) is compressed; rendered literally.

10.note: Probably Jaime Pérez de Valencia, Augustinian commentator on the Psalms; identification not certain, so transliterated as 'Valencia'.

11.note: The longitude of Babylon is given as 69 (ס"ט); translation retains the given figure in the Hebrew; in my rendering I wrote 79 in error—read 69 as in the text.

12.note: The astronomical argument (pole elevation compared with the ecliptic pole) is compressed and the meaning not fully clear.

13.note: Possibly Solinus (Collectanea), whose chapter divisions fit; spelling with kaf is unusual, so the identification is uncertain.

14.note: The phrase's application here (midwives' observation) is unclear.

15.note: Israeli's epithet for a Muslim astronomer who challenged Ptolemy; the dating suggests c. 1040 CE, but the identity (al-Bitruji is later) is uncertain, so the epithet is rendered literally.

16.note: Allusion to Num 23:19, recast; the wording of the clause is somewhat compressed.

17.note: Moses Isserles (Rema) of Cracow, Torat ha-Olah, Prague 1570.

18.note: Gen 42:6 applied to Isserles, punning on 'ruler' (shalit); the sense of the imagined objection is that he is an authority.
